question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent says I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found don't say whether you must be present for a smoke alarm check, and they don't mention a $90 rebooking fee or a 10 am to 12:30 pm weekday window. I can tell you what the law says about entry and fees in general.

**Governing documents (in force on 3 December 2025):**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version **v111**, in force from 25 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version **v005**, in force from 25 November 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says about the situation**

- **Smoke alarms:** The landlord (residential rental provider) must ensure smoke alarms are working and tested at least once every 12 months, following the manufacturer's instructions. Testing or repair of a mains-powered alarm must be done by a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This is the landlord's duty, not yours.
- **Entry:** The landlord may enter to comply with their duties under the Act, and the renter "must allow entry to the premises where the rental provider has followed proper procedure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The excerpts don't say what "proper procedure" requires, such as the notice period.
- **Inspection limits:** The excerpts give different limits on routine inspections. One standard form says "not more than once every 6 months" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), while another says "not more than once every 12 months" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The excerpts don't show which form applies to your agreement, so I can't say which limit applies to you.
- **Fees:** A person must not demand or accept payment from a renter who has failed to comply with the agreement or the Act, other than rent or an amount or penalty provided for in the Act. The penalty for breaching this is 150 penalty units for a natural person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents I found don't contain any provision that allows a $90 rebooking fee for a smoke alarm check. Whether the fee is caught depends on facts I can't verify from these documents.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask the agent for the written notice** of the inspection, including the date, time, and the legal basis for entry. Check whether it follows the entry rules in your agreement.
2. **Ask which provision authorises the $90 fee.** If none is named, you can say the fee is not, as far as the documents show, provided for in the Act.
3. **Ask whether a smoke alarm check requires you to be present.** The documents don't answer this. If you can't attend, you can ask for a different time or for a key arrangement, and put the request in writing.
4. **Contact Consumer Affairs Victoria** for advice. The Regulations list 1300 55 81 81 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) in one form and 1300 558 181 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) in another; both are in the retrieved excerpts.

I'd recommend confirming the exact inspection frequency and notice rules against your signed agreement, since the excerpts don't identify which standard form applies to you.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, at least not for a card fee charged by the app company. Victorian law restricts these fees, but the documents I retrieved don't list every prescribed fee, so the exact position depends on the details.

**What the law says**

- **Fees by a business:** A business other than certain listed persons "must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter in relation to an application to enter into a residential rental agreement or the payment of rent." The penalty is "80 penalty units in the case of a natural person; 400 penalty units in the case of a body corporate" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The listed exempt persons include a residential rental provider, a rental provider's agent, and an authorised deposit taking institution [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text cuts off before the full list, and it does not say which matters are "prescribed" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Fee-free option:** A rental provider or agent "must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available to the renter." The penalty is "80 penalty units in the case of a natural person; 400 penalty units in the case of a body corporate" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The standard agreement form also says the provider "must permit at least one fee-free (other than the renter's own bank fees) payment method" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Electronic payment facilities:** No one may "demand or receive from a renter a charge or indemnity for a charge in relation to... the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent." The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This wording is not limited to the provider or agent, so it may cover a fee taken by a third party.
- **Disclosure:** Before the renter consents to a payment method, the provider or agent must give information about costs the renter may incur, including "third party transaction fees" and "any other electronic payment facility fees" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Does it matter who gets the fee?**

Yes, somewhat:

- **Fee to the app company:** The app company is not one of the listed exempt persons in the retrieved text, so s 51A(1) appears to apply to it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Section 51(3)(b) also applies to any person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Fee to the agent:** The agent is a listed exempt person under s 51A(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), so s 51A does not apply to the agent's own fee. However, s 51(3)(b) still applies to "a person" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), and the agent must ensure a fee-free method is reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The agent also has the disclosure duty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

Whether a card payment fee counts as a charge for an "electronic payment facility" under s 51(3)(b) is an interpretation question. The documents do not address it directly.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask in writing** whether the card fee is charged, who receives it, and how much it is. The provider or agent must give cost information before you choose a payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. **Use the fee-free method.** The law requires a no-extra-cost method to be "reasonably available" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Bank transfer appears to meet this, even though it is slower. The documents don't say whether slowness affects "reasonably available."
3. **Check your agreement.** Rent is paid in the manner specified in the agreement, and the parties can change that by agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
4. **Keep records.** The renter can ask for a receipt. If a receipt is requested, it must be given within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

The documents do not cover how to make a complaint or how to enforce these rules (for example, through the Tribunal or a regulator). I can't say from these sources what your remedies are.

**Version applied:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (version 111, in force 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (S.R. No. 3/2021, version 005, in force 25 November 2025 to 9 February 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Both were in force on 15 January 2026.

This is general information based on the retrieved text, not legal advice. If you're unsure, a tenancy service can confirm how the rules apply to your app.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the Act as it stood on 15 October 2019, you have grounds to refuse to move in, to demand repairs, and possibly to withhold rent. Whether the newer rules apply depends on when your lease was entered into, which the documents don't tell me.

**Which version applies:** The retrieved document is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version **No. 088**, file "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf" dated 2 July 2019. Its metadata shows it was in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019, so it covers 15 October 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**Caveat on the 2018 amendments:** This version includes changes from the *Residential Tenancies Amendment Act 2018*, which are the source of "renter," "residential rental provider," and the rental minimum standards. However, the transitional provisions say the new sections, including s 65A, do not apply to agreements entered into before the applicable amendment commenced, until those agreements end [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't state the commencement date, so I can't confirm whether those new rules govern your lease. Where I describe the new rules below, that caveat applies.

---

### What the law says

- **Premises must be ready on move-in day.** The landlord must ensure that, on the day the tenant is to enter occupation, the premises are vacant and reasonably clean. A tenant is not required to move into premises that don't comply, and no rent is payable for the period between the agreed move-in day and the day the tenant actually moves in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Duty to maintain.** The landlord must keep the premises in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Under the amended version, the landlord must also keep them "in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation," and this applies whether or not the renter was aware of the disrepair before moving in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Rental minimum standards.** Under the amended version, the landlord must ensure the premises comply with prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day you enter occupation (penalty: 60 penalty units for an individual, 300 for a body corporate) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Mould and damp.** The amended definition of "urgent repairs" includes "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Rotting timber may fall under the general repair duty, but the documents don't say so expressly.

### Your options

**1. Cancel the agreement**
- Under the amended Division 9, a residential rental agreement terminates if the renter has not yet taken possession and gives notice of termination on the ground that the premises "are not in good repair," "are unfit for human habitation," or "do not meet any rental minimum standards" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The landlord's own right to terminate before possession is limited to premises that are unfit for habitation or destroyed or unsafe [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The documents I retrieved don't include the full text of the older pre-possession termination provision (s 226), so I can't set out its notice requirements.

**2. Ask for repairs**
- **Urgent repairs:** You may arrange urgent repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to do them immediately and cannot. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost. Under the amended version, you must give written notice of the repairs and their cost, and the landlord must reimburse within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The old version required 14 days' notice and capped reimbursement at $1,000, but the amendment removed that cap [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Written notice first:** You must report damage and breakdowns to the landlord in writing as soon as practicable (amended s 72AA) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** Give the landlord written notice. If repairs are not carried out within 14 days, you may apply to the Director of Housing to investigate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You may then apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal orders:** The Tribunal can order the landlord to carry out specified repairs within a specified time, and the amended version allows compensation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**3. Ask for lower rent or withhold rent**
- **No rent before move-in:** If the premises don't meet the move-in requirements, you don't have to pay rent for the period before you actually move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Rent into the Rent Special Account:** After giving written notice requiring repairs, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order to pay rent into the Rent Special Account if the landlord has failed to carry out repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Excessive rent:** The Tribunal may find rent is more than should reasonably be paid, having regard to "the state of repair and general condition of the rented premises." It can order a reduction and a refund of the difference [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

---

### What the documents don't cover

- The commencement date of the 2018 amendments, and therefore whether they apply to your lease.
- The exact date you signed the lease.
- Whether damp and mould count as "not reasonably clean" under the move-in provision.
- The Director's guidelines, which the Tribunal must consider in urgent-repair cases [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The current rental minimum standards regulations, which are prescribed elsewhere.

Given these gaps, I'd recommend confirming with a tenancy advice service before taking formal steps, such as serving notice or cancelling.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the Act, the rent payment method is set by your agreement, and it can be changed only by agreement between you and the provider. Before paying into the new account, confirm the change in writing, check the new method is fee-free for you, and confirm your bond is still held properly. The documents don't say how to verify that a bank account really belongs to the owner.

The Act in force on 8 November 2022 is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. 101, in force from 7 September 2022) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version No. 002, in force from 1 June 2022) also apply [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Payment method is part of the agreement.** Rent is payable at the place in the agreement, or at the premises if none is specified, and otherwise in the manner the agreement specifies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The provider and renter, by agreement, may change the manner in which rent is payable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). A unilateral change is not provided for.
- **Costs and fees.** The provider or agent must give you information about any costs (including third-party transaction fees and direct debit dishonour fees) before you consent to a payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). A payment method with no additional costs, other than your bank or account fees, must be reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Permitted methods.** The provider must allow Centrepay, and the prescribed method is electronic funds transfer [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Post-dated cheques cannot be required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Receipts.** For a non-cash payment, a written receipt must be given within 5 business days of receipt if you request one. It must be signed and state your name and the premises, the date, the period paid for, the amount, and that the payment is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Notice of changes.** The provider must give you written notice of any change to the agent's or provider's contact details before the end of 7 days after the change [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The standard form says the same: the rental provider must notify the renter within 7 days if this information changes [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Bond.** The provider or agent must lodge the bond with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) within 10 business days after receiving it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The RTBA must send you a receipt within 7 days of receiving the bond [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). If you have not received a receipt within 15 business days of paying, you may email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call 1300 137 164 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What to check and ask for

1. **Get the change in writing and agreed.** Ask for written confirmation of the new payment details and your agreement to use them. Under the Act, the change needs your agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Confirm the account holder and who is the provider.** Ask for the owner's full legal name. The 7-day notice rule applies to changes in the provider's and agent's details [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask about fees.** Before you consent, ask what costs the new method involves. Make sure at least one method is free of charges other than your own bank fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Check the bond.** Confirm the bond was lodged with the RTBA and that you were given a receipt. If not, you can contact the RTBA as described above [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Keep receipts.** Request a signed rent receipt that meets the s 43 requirements [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
6. **Check for transfers.** If the rights and duties under the agreement are being transferred to another person, a notice must be given to the RTBA within 5 days, signed by all parties, and you must be given a copy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

The documents do not say how to verify a bank account, what to do about suspected payment fraud, or whether the agent's authority has ended. They also don't set out whether you must stop paying the agent. question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent says I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say whether you must be personally present. They do not allow the agent to charge a $90 rebooking fee for this, but they also don't expressly prohibit it. Under the version in force on 3 December 2025, the rules are as follows.

**Versions applied:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (version 111, in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (version 005, in force from 25 November 2025 to 9 February 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) both cover 3 December 2025.

## What the law says

- **Duty to permit entry:** A renter has a duty to permit a person exercising a right of entry under the Act to enter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Entry is allowed for a duty under the Act:** The provider or agent may enter to carry out a duty under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Smoke alarms must be tested at least once every 12 months in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Mains-powered alarms must be tested by a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Time and notice:** Entry for this purpose is allowed at any time between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day except a public holiday, if at least 24 hours' notice has been given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The notice must be in writing, state why entry is needed, and be given by post or delivered personally between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Manner of entry:** The person must act in a reasonable manner and must not stay longer than necessary without your consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Regulations:** The provider may enter to comply with their duties under the Act, and "the renter must allow entry to the premises where the rental provider has followed proper procedure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

## Your questions

**1. Do I have to be there myself?**
The documents don't say. They establish your duty to permit entry where proper procedure is followed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), but they don't state that you must personally attend. Note also that the Act doesn't limit entry to weekdays. It allows any day except a public holiday, between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Your agent's 10 a.m.–12:30 p.m. weekday window is not set out in these documents.

**2. Can they charge $90 to rebook?**
The documents don't address this. The only fee provision I found is section 51(2), which bars charging a renter for inspecting premises under a proposed agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). That doesn't cover a smoke alarm check under an existing tenancy. I found no reference to a $90 rebooking fee.

## What you can do or ask

- **Check the notice:** Confirm it is in writing, gives the reason for entry, and gives at least 24 hours' notice within the permitted hours [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask for an agreed time:** Entry at a time agreed with you is permitted if you consented within the 7 days before entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask for the fee's legal basis:** Ask the agent which provision allows the $90 charge. The documents don't provide one.
- **Apply to VCAT:** You may apply to the Tribunal for an order specifying or limiting the days, times and purposes of entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

If you want a firm answer on personal attendance or the fee, the documents you've provided don't contain it, so you'd need to check with Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the documents I have, the app probably cannot charge you a card fee for rent without restriction, and the answer depends partly on who receives the fee. One point is unresolved: the documents don't show whether a surcharge is permitted under another Act.

I've applied the versions in force on 15 January 2026: the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 111 (in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 005 (in force from 25 November 2025 to 9 February 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). These are the version numbers shown in the document metadata.

## What the law says

- **Fee-free method must be available:** A provider or agent must ensure that a rent payment method with no additional costs, other than the renter's own bank or account fees, is reasonably available to the renter. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Cost disclosure:** Before you consent to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur, including third-party transaction fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Fee to anyone for using electronic payment:** No person may demand or receive a charge for the establishment or use of direct debit or any other electronic payment facility for rent. The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A card fee may fall within this, though the documents don't define "electronic payment facility."
- **Application and rent payment fees:** A business other than a provider, agent, or authorised deposit-taking institution must not demand or receive a fee for a prescribed matter relating to rent payment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Providers and agents are excluded from this rule [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The regulations list "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)" as a prescribed matter, but this only has effect from 31 March 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). So on 15 January 2026, that listed prohibition is not yet in force.
- **Bank transfer:** The prescribed payment method is electronic funds transfer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The standard terms note that the provider must permit a fee-free method (other than the renter's own bank fees) and must allow Centrepay or another form of electronic funds transfer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

## Does it matter who gets the fee?

Yes, in two ways:

- **Fee to the app company:** The app company is not a provider, agent, or authorised deposit-taking institution, so the s 51A prohibition could apply to it. However, the documents don't say what "payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act" covers, so I can't confirm whether a card surcharge falls within that exception.
- **Fee to the agent:** Agents are excluded from s 51A [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), but the agent must still make a fee-free method reasonably available and disclose costs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't say whether your app is the provider's agent, so I can't tell which rule applies to your specific arrangement.

## What you can do

1. **Ask for the bank transfer option in writing.** Under the law, a fee-free method must be reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The slower speed of bank transfer doesn't by itself make it unavailable.
2. **Ask for written details of every cost** of the card option before you agree to use it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check your agreement.** Rent is payable in the manner specified in the agreement, but this can be changed by agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The regulations also list a term requiring rent in advance by a payment method with additional costs (other than bank or account fees) as a prohibited term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
4. **Ask for a receipt.** If you request one at the time of payment, you're entitled to a written receipt within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't cover how to make a complaint or what remedies apply, so for those steps you'd need other sources.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Version applied:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 088 (incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019). The retrieved copy is marked as in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019, so it covers 15 October 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). This is a general summary, not legal advice.

## What the law says

- **Condition on move-in:** On the day the tenant is due to enter occupation, the landlord must ensure the premises are vacant and in a reasonably clean condition. If they are not, the tenant is not required to move in, and is not required to pay rent for the period between the agreed day and the day they actually enter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 65).
- **Repairs:** The landlord must ensure the premises are maintained in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 68(1)). The retrieved text also includes an amendment that would require premises to be "in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation," apply whether or not the renter knew of the disrepair, and have an express reference to mould or damp [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). However, the documents don't clearly confirm when that amendment took effect, so I can't confirm it applied on 15 October 2019.
- **Condition report:** If you paid a bond, the landlord must give you a signed condition report before you move in. Within 3 business days after entering occupation, you must return a copy signed, or with an endorsement saying you agree or disagree with all or part of it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (ss 35(1)–(2)). A signed report is conclusive evidence of the state of repair, except for defects that could not reasonably have been discovered on a reasonable inspection, or statements you disagree with under an endorsement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 36).

## Your options

**1. Cancel**
- The tenancy ends if you have not entered into possession and you give the landlord a notice of termination on the ground that the premises are not in good repair or are unfit for human habitation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 226).
- **Caveat:** The documents don't define "entered into possession." Picking up keys may or may not count, so check this before relying on it. If you have already moved in, this option may not apply.

**2. Ask for repairs**
- **Notify in writing:** The renter must give written notice to the landlord as soon as practicable after becoming aware of damage or breakdown of facilities [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (amendment inserting s 72AA).
- **Urgent repairs:** You may arrange urgent repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to do them immediately and cannot. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost **or $1000, whichever is less**, and you must give 14 days' written notice of the repairs and cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 72). The Tribunal can order urgent repairs, and must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 73). Damp and mould are only "urgent" if they make the premises unsafe or insecure under the urgent repairs definition [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** Give written notice of the repairs. If the landlord doesn't carry them out within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 74(1)). You can then apply to the Tribunal for a repair order, but only after receiving the Director's report, and within 60 days of receiving it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (ss 75(1)–(2)). The Tribunal can order specified repairs and set a deadline [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 76).

**3. Ask for lower rent**
- The documents do **not** contain a provision that lets you unilaterally reduce rent because of disrepair. Please don't reduce rent without advice.
- Rent is not payable for the period before you enter occupation if the premises fail the move-in standard in s 65 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The state of repair is a factor the Tribunal must consider when deciding if rent is excessive [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 47(3)(b)). An application to the Director must be made within 30 days after a rent increase notice, and a tenant can then apply to the Tribunal within 30 days after the Director's report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (ss 45(2), 46(1)–(2)). These provisions concern rent increases and excessive rent, not a reduction for current disrepair.
- If the landlord fails to carry out required repairs, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order authorising you to pay rent into the Rent Special Account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 77(1)–(2)).

## Practical steps
- Photograph everything and keep a dated record.
- Give the landlord written notice of each defect now.
- If there is a condition report, check it and endorse any disagreement within 3 business days of moving in.

## What the documents don't cover
- Whether picking up the keys counts as "entering into possession."
- Commencement dates for the amendments on mould, damp, and the move-in standards.
- Tribunal fees, timelines beyond those quoted above, and the Director's guidelines.

For these points, check with Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT, or get legal advice.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say how to verify a new payee's bank account. They do set out what the agent or owner must do when rent payment arrangements or contact details change, and what you're entitled to. Those rules are below.

I've applied the versions in force on 8 November 2022: the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf, version 101, in force from 7 September 2022) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf, version 002, in force from 1 June 2022) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Where rent is paid:** Rent is payable at the place specified in your agreement, or at the rented premises if none is specified [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **How rent is paid:** Rent is payable in the manner specified in the agreement. The landlord and renter can change the manner of payment, but only by agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Payment costs:** The provider or agent must ensure a payment method with no extra costs (other than your own bank or account fees) is reasonably available. They must also give you information about any costs of a payment method before you agree to use it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Centrepay and EFT:** The provider or agent must permit Centrepay, and electronic funds transfer is the prescribed payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Changes to agent or owner details:** If an agent is acting, the provider must give you written notice of the agent's details. Any change must be notified in writing before the end of 7 days after the change, with a penalty of 60 penalty units for failing to do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The standard agreement form says the same [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Receipts:** Anyone receiving rent must give a written receipt. For payments not made in person, this is required within 5 business days if you request one. The receipt must be signed and state your name and the premises, the date, the period paid, the amount, and that the payment is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Bond:** The provider or agent must lodge the bond with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) within 10 business days after receiving it. If you don't receive an RTBA receipt within 15 business days, you may email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call 1300 137 164 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What to check before paying the new account

1. **Written confirmation of the change.** Ask for the change in writing, including the new account details and who is the rental provider.
2. **Agreed payment method.** Check that the new arrangement is one you agreed to in writing, as the Act allows changes to the payment method by agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Fees.** Ask what costs, if any, apply to this payment method. You're entitled to that information before you agree to use it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Notice of the new contact details.** The owner or agent should give you written notice of any change to their details, within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Bond still held.** Confirm your bond is still lodged with the RTBA and that you can get a receipt [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If the property's ownership is transferred, the parties must notify the Authority within 5 days of the transfer taking effect [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

**Short answer:** The documents don't say you must be home. They also don't address a $90 rebooking fee for a smoke alarm check, so I can't confirm whether that fee is lawful.

Regulation 30A says the same thing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Entry for a legal duty:** Entry to carry out a duty under the Act is allowed between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day except a public holiday, with at least 24 hours' notice to the renter [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

- **Renter's duty:** The renter must permit entry that follows these rules, and the inspector must act in a reasonable manner and not stay longer than necessary without consent [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not. Under the Act as it stands on 15 January 2026, a person generally cannot charge you for paying rent by an electronic payment facility. The recipient matters less than you might expect, though it affects which rule applies.

## What the law says

- **The governing documents:** I'm relying on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (version 111, in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (version 005, in force from 25 November 2025 to 9 February 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Both cover 15 January 2026.
- **No charge for electronic payment facilities:** A person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge "in relation to... the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent." The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A card payment facility appears to fall within this, but the documents don't say how it applies to every app fee structure.
- **Provider or agent must offer a free method:** The provider or agent must ensure a payment method that incurs no additional costs is reasonably available. The only exceptions are bank fees or account fees on the renter's own bank account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Manual bank transfer, if fee-free, would meet this.
- **Cost disclosure:** Before you agree to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about costs, including third-party transaction fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Rent-payment fee ban (not yet in force):** Section 51A bans businesses other than the provider, agent, or a deposit-taking institution from charging a fee for a prescribed matter in relation to rent payment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). However, the regulation listing those prescribed matters says it "has effect on and after 31 March 2026," so it does not apply on 15 January 2026. Its list also excludes "payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The documents don't identify any such Act.

## Does it matter who gets the fee?

- **Yes, for section 51A:** The provider and agent are exempt from section 51A, but an app company is not [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This rule isn't yet operative for rent-payment fees, however.
- **No, for section 51(3)(b):** This prohibition applies to "a person," so it isn't limited to agents or app companies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **The agent's duties still apply:** Even if the fee goes to the app, the agent must ensure a free method is reasonably available and must disclose costs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the agent in writing** whether a fee-free method (such as bank transfer or Centrepay) is available, and what costs apply to the card option [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for a receipt** if you pay by a non-in-person method. You can request it at the time of payment and it must be given within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. **Pay by the free method** while the dispute is open. Note that the documents don't say whether the slower timing causes any issue for late-payment purposes.
4. **Check the agreement:** A term requiring you to pay rent by a method with extra costs (other than your own bank fees) is a prescribed prohibited term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't set out how to make a complaint, how to recover a fee already paid, or what happens if the app's fee is later found to be a permitted surcharge. For those steps, you'd need other sources, such as Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT guidance.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Document relied on:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version **No. 088** (file "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf"; in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019 per its metadata [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)). That covers 15 October 2019.

## What the law says

- **Premises must be ready on the move-in day.** The landlord must ensure that on the agreed occupation day the premises are "vacant and in a reasonably clean condition." A tenant is not required to move in if they don't comply, and rent is not payable from the agreed day until the tenant actually enters occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The document does not define "reasonably clean," so it is unclear whether mould or rot falls under this.
- **Ongoing repair duty.** The landlord "must ensure that the rented premises are maintained in good repair" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Mould and damp count as urgent repairs.** The document sets out an amendment that defines urgent repairs to include "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The excerpt does not show the commencement date of this amendment, so check that before relying on it.
- **Termination before possession.** A tenancy agreement terminates if the tenant "has not entered into possession" and gives notice of termination on the ground that the premises "are not in good repair" or "are unfit for human habitation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). A parallel provision in the amended Division 9 uses the word "renter" and includes "do not meet any rental minimum standards" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## Your options

**1. Cancel.** Your best route is termination before possession, but only if you have not yet "entered into possession." The documents do not define possession, so having the keys may or may not count. If you have not moved in, you may give a termination notice on the ground that the house is not in good repair or is unfit for habitation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Once you are living there, cancellation options are narrower. A renter may give a notice of intention to vacate where the premises are "unfit for human habitation," with a termination date on or after the notice date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**2. Ask for repairs.**
- **Report in writing.** A renter must give written notice to the landlord "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs.** If the landlord cannot be got to act, the renter may arrange urgent repairs after taking reasonable steps. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost, capped at $1000 under the current wording, within 7 days of written notice of the repairs and their cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The documents state the cap as "$1000, or if a greater amount is prescribed" in the wording being amended, so check the current prescribed amount.
- **Non-urgent repairs.** If the landlord has not carried out repairs "within 14 days after receiving the notice," you may apply to the Director to investigate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You may also apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) for an order requiring specified repairs. The Tribunal "must hear an application... within 7 days" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Rent into the Rent Special Account.** The Tribunal may order rent paid into the Rent Special Account if a notice requiring repairs has been given and the landlord has failed to comply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**3. Ask for lower rent.** The documents do not provide a direct power to reduce rent for defects. The options they do contain are:
- **No rent until move-in.** Rent is not payable for the period before you actually enter occupation if the premises do not comply on the agreed day [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Compensation.** The Tribunal may order compensation for loss suffered from a breach, and the compensation "may specify... a refund or reduction of the rent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Excessive rent.** The Tribunal may declare rent excessive, and one factor is "the state of repair and general condition of the rented premises" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). This process is aimed mainly at rent increases.

## Gaps

- The documents do not say whether having the keys counts as "entering into possession."
- They do not define "reasonably clean" or confirm whether mould and rot fall under it.
- They do not confirm the commencement date of the amendments that refer to "renter" and mould/damp.

Given these gaps, consider getting advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advocate before you give any notice.

(2) It states the landlord 'must ensure that the rented premises are maintained in good repair', describes how to report and request repairs, and covers urgent repairs, including mould and damp. (3) It ties cancellation to disrepair or unfitness ('you may give a termination notice on the ground that the house is not in good repair or is unfit for habitation') and keeps this separate from the 'reasonably clean' rule, which only lets the tenant decline to move in and delays rent. question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the Act, the payment arrangement in your lease can only be changed by agreement, and the new details must not cost you extra fees. Before paying, get the change confirmed in writing and check the points below.

I've applied the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 101, in force 7 September 2022 to 23 May 2023) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version No. 002, in force 1 June 2022 to 30 November 2024) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Both were in force on 8 November 2022.

## What the law says

- **The lease sets the payment method, and changes need agreement.** Rent is payable at the place in the agreement, or at the premises if none is specified, and in the manner the agreement specifies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The provider and renter can change the manner of payment by agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The owner cannot unilaterally switch you to a new account.
- **No extra costs.** The provider or agent must ensure a payment method with no additional costs, other than your own bank or account fees, is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Before you consent to a payment method, they must tell you about any costs, including third-party transaction fees and direct debit dishonour fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Permitted methods.** The provider must allow payment by Centrepay and by electronic funds transfer, which is the prescribed method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Receipts.** If rent is not paid in person, you can request a receipt, and it must be given within 5 business days. It must be signed and state your name and the premises, the date, the period paid, the amount, and that the payment is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Changes to agent or contact details.** Written notice of changes must be given within 7 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The lease form says the provider must notify you within 7 days if the agent's details change [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Failing to give this notice carries a penalty of 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Bond.** If the owner takes over the rights and duties under the agreement from someone else, the notice requirements in section 424 apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The agent must lodge the bond with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) within 10 business days of receiving it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can check or ask for

1. **Written agreement to the change.** Ask for written confirmation of the new account and that you have agreed to it. Do not treat an emailed account change alone as a valid variation without confirming it.
2. **Who the payee is.** Confirm the account holder is the owner named in your lease, and check the owner's identity through contact details you already hold, not only those in the new message.
3. **Fees.** Ask whether the new method has any cost to you beyond your own bank fees, and get that in writing before you agree [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
4. **A fee-free option.** Confirm you still have a fee-free method available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Written notice of the new contact and agent details.** Ask for written notice of the change in management [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
6. **Receipts.** Ask for a receipt for each payment, and keep your bank records [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
7. **Bond.** Check that your bond is still registered with the RTBA and that you have the RTBA receipt [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
8. **Ownership change.** If the owner has sold or transferred the property, ask whether a bond notification under section 424 has been made [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

They also don't say what to do if the owner refuses to provide written confirmation. For general guidance, the lease summary points renters to consumer.vic.gov.au/renting [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
